MAPThe test ladder: each step sees smaller, but loses something

LO 1Principles of molecular cytogenetics

Q1. What can a conventional karyotype do, and where does it fall short?

Pros

  • Detects changes in chromosome number
  • Detects large structural changes (deletions, duplications, insertions, translocations)
  • Sees balanced rearrangements
  • Cheap

Cons

  • Low resolution (~5–10 Mb): small deletions missed
  • Needs cells in metaphase
  • Needs culture; slow (10–14 days)
Q2. How does FISH work?
  1. Design a single-stranded DNA probe complementary to the region, tagged with a fluorophore
  2. Denature (heat) the patient's DNA into single strands
  3. Cool → probe hybridizes to its complement
  4. Wash away unbound probe
  5. Read under a fluorescence microscope

FISH principle

  • Labeled probe finds its complementary target

Pros

  • High sensitivity for the target
  • Detects large and micro changes
  • Works in any cell-cycle stage (interphase too)
  • Detects mosaicism

Cons

  • Only finds what you probe for
  • An unexpected abnormality elsewhere is missed
High yield

FISH extended cytogenetics from metaphase chromosomes to all stages of the cell cycle: interphase analysis shows morphology and genetic change in the same cell.

Analogy — glowing magnets

Each probe is a glowing magnet for one address. Count the dots (copy number), look for a missing dot (deletion), a merged dot (fusion) or a cluster (amplification).

Q3. What are the FISH probe types?

Four probe types

  • Centromeric · telomeric · locus-specific · paint
ProbeBindsUse
CentromericChromosome-specific centromere repeatsCount chromosomes (aneuploidy), even in interphase
TelomericChromosome endsSubtle terminal deletions/rearrangements
Locus-specificOne gene/regionMicrodeletions (22q11.2), fusions (BCR-ABL), amplification (HER2)
Whole-chromosome paintPool of fragments covering a chromosomeTranslocations; multicolor FISH / SKY (all 24)
In-house exam

Match the probe to the question: centromeric → aneuploidy; locus-specific → microdeletion, fusion, amplification; paint → translocation.

Q4. How does chromosomal microarray (array CGH) work?
  1. Label test DNA one color (green) and reference DNA another (red); mix 1:1
  2. Hybridize to an array of DNA sequences spanning the genome
  3. Scanner reads the ratio at each spot
RatioColorMeaning
EqualYellowNormal copy number (plot at 0)
Test > referenceGreenGain (plot rises)
Test < referenceRedLoss (plot drops)

Array CGH method

  • Two colors, one chip, ratio plot

Trisomy 13

  • Gain across the whole chromosome

15q11.2–q13.1 deletion

  • Line drops = loss

Can detect

  • Deletions/duplications of any size, down to exon level
  • Aneuploidy
  • Microdeletions (15q11.2, 22q11.2)
  • Regions of homozygosity (SNP arrays)
  • Needs DNA only: no metaphase, no culture

Cannot detect

  • Balanced rearrangements (translocation, inversion)
  • Location of extra material (free vs Robertsonian trisomy)
  • Low-level mosaicism
  • Point mutations
High yield — why microarray misses balanced changes

The DNA is chopped up. Total copy number is unchanged in a balanced translocation, so it looks normal, and you can't tell where extra material sits.

Trap

A 15q11.2–q13.1 deletion on array can't distinguish Prader-Willi vs Angelman: that needs parent-of-origin (methylation) studies.

Step 1

SNP arrays show long regions of homozygosity: uniparental isodisomy or consanguinity.

ApplyLO 1 application questions

A1A couple has had three miscarriages; both parents' microarrays are normal. Is a chromosomal cause excluded?
No: microarray misses balanced translocations. Order parental karyotypes.
A2A microarray shows a gain of all of chromosome 21. Is it free or Robertsonian trisomy?
Microarray can't tell (no location). Order a karyotype; it matters for recurrence risk.

LO 2Diagnostic applications

Q1. How is FISH used to find a microdeletion?
  • Microdeletions are usually <5 Mb → missed by G-banding; seen by FISH, array CGH or sometimes high-resolution karyotype
  • Probe cocktail: 22q11.2 test probe (orange) + 22q13 control (green)
  • 2 control + 2 test = normal; 2 control + 1 test = del(22)(q11.2) → DiGeorge / velocardiofacial syndrome

22q11.2 probe cocktail

  • Test (orange) + control (green)

22q11.2 deletion

  • Arrow: chromosome 22 missing the test signal
Step 1

22q11.2 deletion = CATCH-22: Cardiac (conotruncal), Abnormal facies, Thymic aplasia (T-cell deficiency), Cleft palate, Hypocalcemia (parathyroid aplasia).

Trap

FISH is targeted: a normal 22q11.2 FISH doesn't rule out a deletion elsewhere. When the cause is unknown, microarray is preferred (and it sizes the deletion).

Q2. How is FISH used for translocations and aneuploidy?

Translocations (paints)

  • A paint color on another chromosome = translocation
  • Shows approximate size, not the exact sequence
  • Multicolor FISH / SKY: 24 paints at once → markers, complex rearrangements

Aneuploidy (centromeric, interphase)

  • 3 signals = trisomic; 2 = disomic
  • Works on uncultured cells (amniotic fluid), fixed tumor sections, low-mitotic samples (chemo, post-BMT)
  • Fast: ~48–72 h vs 10–14 days

Whole-chromosome paints

  • Chromosomes 1 and 3 reveal an exchange

Spectral karyotype

  • All 24 chromosomes in different colors

Interphase centromeric FISH

  • Trisomy 18 male · normal 13/21 · trisomy 21
High yield

Rapid prenatal FISH on amniocytes should be confirmed by karyotype or microarray before irreversible decisions.

Q3. When is microarray the first-tier test?

Postnatal (ACMG 2010)

  • Multiple anomalies not specific to a known syndrome
  • Apparently nonsyndromic developmental delay / ID
  • Autism spectrum disorder
  • Follow-up of an imbalance: FISH/cytogenetics, parental studies, counseling

Prenatal (ACOG)

  • ≥1 major structural anomaly + invasive testing → microarray (replaces karyotype)
  • Structurally normal fetus → karyotype or microarray
  • Not restricted to women ≥35 (findings mostly not age-related)
  • Stillbirth → microarray on fetal tissue
  • Pre/post-test counseling + consent (uncertain findings, non-paternity, consanguinity)
Memory tool — stillbirth

Karyotype needs living cells to culture; dead tissue often won't grow. Microarray needs DNA only.

Q4. How is FISH used in cancer?

CML: BCR-ABL

  • Every CML has a BCR (22q11)–ABL (9q34) fusion: t(9;22), Philadelphia chromosome
  • 95% visible on karyotype (simple or complex)
  • 5% submicroscopic ("masked"): normal karyotype, FISH or RT-PCR positive
  • FISH: ABL green, BCR red → fusion = yellow

Breast cancer: HER2/NEU

  • Locus-specific HER2 (17q12) probe + chromosome 17 control on fixed tumor
  • Normal: 2 HER2 + 2 control; amplified: many HER2 signals
  • More aggressive; guides trastuzumab

Philadelphia karyotype

  • 46,XY,t(9;22)(q34;q11.2)

BCR-ABL FISH

  • Separate ABL + BCR, plus one yellow fusion

CML detection

  • Fusion signal on der(22) = Ph chromosome

HER2 FISH

  • Amplified = clusters of red HER2 signals
In-house exam

Classic CML with a normal karyotype → order BCR-ABL FISH (or RT-PCR): ~5% have a masked fusion. Don't call it "Ph-negative CML" first.

Step 1

HER2 FISH is used when IHC is equivocal (2+); HER2/CEP17 ratio ≥2.0 = amplified. BCR-ABL FISH/PCR also monitors TKI (imatinib) response.

Q5. Which test do I pick?
QuestionBest test
Balanced translocation / recurrent miscarriageKaryotype
Free vs Robertsonian trisomyKaryotype
Suspected specific microdeletionFISH or microarray (microarray sizes it)
DD/ID, autism, multiple anomaliesMicroarray first-tier
Fetal structural anomalyMicroarray (replaces karyotype)
StillbirthMicroarray on fetal tissue
Rapid aneuploidy on amniocytes; non-dividing marrowInterphase FISH
CML with normal karyotypeBCR-ABL FISH / RT-PCR
HER2 status, equivocal IHCHER2 FISH
Point mutation (CFTR)Sequencing
PWS vs AngelmanMethylation studies

ApplyLO 2 application questions

A1A 32-week stillborn fetus's skin culture failed to grow. Best test for a chromosomal cause?
Microarray on fetal tissue or placenta (DNA only, no culture).
A2A patient on chemotherapy needs a chromosome count, but the marrow cells won't divide. Which test?
Interphase FISH with centromeric probes.

IDImage ID

Image 1 — metaphase FISH
One chromosome 22 lacks the test signal → 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge/VCFS).
Image 2 — interphase nuclei
Centromeric FISH: 3 signals = trisomy (18; 21).
Image 3 — plot
Microarray gain across chromosome 13 → trisomy 13.
Image 4 — plot
Microarray loss at 15q11.2–q13.1 → needs methylation for PWS vs AS.
Image 5 — nucleus
Yellow fusion signal → BCR-ABL (CML).
Image 6 — tumor nuclei
HER2 amplification → trastuzumab.
Image 7 — colored chromosomes
Spectral karyotype (multicolor FISH, 24 paints).

MCQExam-style questions

Score: 0 / 0

1An infant has a conotruncal heart defect, cleft palate and hypocalcemia. FISH with a 22q11.2 test probe and a 22q13 control probe shows two control signals and one test signal. Interpretation?

One chromosome 22 lacks the test region → DiGeorge/VCFS.

2Which abnormality will a chromosomal microarray miss?

Total copy number unchanged → looks normal.

3A 4-year-old has nonsyndromic developmental delay and autism. Recommended first-tier genetic test?

ACMG: CMA first-tier for DD/ID, autism, multiple anomalies.

4A couple has had three first-trimester losses. Which parental test best looks for a chromosomal cause?

Looking for a balanced translocation carrier.

5An amniocentesis is done at 18 weeks; the family wants a rapid answer about trisomy 21. Which test gives the fastest result on uncultured cells?

No culture needed; confirm with karyotype or microarray.

6A fetus has a major cardiac anomaly on ultrasound, and the mother chooses amniocentesis. Per ACOG, which test is recommended?

Microarray replaces karyotype with a structural anomaly.

7A 45-year-old has splenomegaly, WBC 150,000/µL with all stages of granulocytes, and basophilia. Karyotype is 46,XY with no visible t(9;22). Next step?

~5% of CML has a masked, submicroscopic fusion.

8A breast cancer is HER2 2+ (equivocal) by IHC. FISH shows many HER2 signals per nucleus relative to the chromosome 17 control. Implication?

Amplification → aggressive, targeted therapy.

9Why is microarray preferred over karyotype after a stillbirth?

Dead tissue often fails culture.

10A microarray shows a deletion at 15q11.2–q13.1 in a hypotonic infant. Which test distinguishes Prader-Willi from Angelman?

Microarray shows copy number, not parent of origin.

11Which FISH probe type is best for identifying an unknown marker chromosome or a complex translocation?

24 paints identify every chromosome's material.

12A microarray shows a gain of the whole of chromosome 21. What additional information requires a karyotype?

Location of extra material → recurrence risk.
